paragraphs.text: AGAINST THOSE WHO DELAY BAPTISM. When the kings of this world draw up laws that rightly regulate human life, they hand them to their governors and order them to be published to their subjects through them, so that what has been commanded may be kept unbroken. In the same way the great God has given laws to the leaders of the Churches. Each year, at the proper seasons, we bring them out, read them to you, and urge you to keep what is written as far as you are able. See, then: the good steward of all things, who turns the years round and steers the cycle of the seasons, has brought the day of salvation. On this day it is our custom to call strangers to adoption, the poor to a share in grace, and those who are fouled with offenses to the cleansing of their sins. And this is that ancient proclamation which came a little before the Saviour's appearing: "A voice of one crying

in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." I am neither John nor David, but do not let the lowliness of the servant weaken the force of the Master's law. We do not obey what has been decreed out of respect for the clerks who write the laws down. We bow to the commands because we fear the authority of the Lawgiver. Royal grace has come, granting relief to two classes of afflicted people: release to prisoners, and remission to debtors. For this reason I too open clinics suited to both classes, and with great confidence I promise the help that comes from care. And so that no one thinks the treatment costly, I will tell you in advance the very remedies by which I heal the sick [?]. To some I guarantee health through water and washing, and for others I wipe out the disease with a few tears. The treatment is simple, the gift is sent by God, and the success is truly great: to be rid of chronic wounds without cautery or the knife, wounds we wretchedly suffered from the bites of the serpent. Come, then, you who are afflicted, and take care of yourselves. Do not leave the matter to sloth, for a disease that has grown old and chronic becomes too strong for the art of healing. You poor and needy, hurry to the distribution of the royal gifts. You sheep, hurry to the seal and the sign of the cross, the defense against evils. Give me your names, so that I may inscribe them in books the senses can see and write them in ink, while God engraves them on incorruptible tablets, writing with his own finger, as he once wrote the law for the Hebrews. "Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed." "Wash yourselves, take away your sins." These words were written long ago, but their power has not grown old. It is in full flower and strong every day. Come out of the prison, I beg you. Hate the dark dwellings of sin. Flee the devil as a cruel jailer who feeds and profits on the misfortune of sinners. For as God rejoices in our righteous deeds, so the author of sin delights in our transgressions. You are outside paradise, catechumen, sharing exile with Adam our forefather. But now the door is being opened for you. Go back in where you came out, and do not delay, or death may fall upon you and block the entrance. Your head is already turning white and the harvest of your life is near. Perhaps the sickle is already being sharpened against us, and I fear that while we sleep and busy ourselves with empty vanities, the dread reaper may suddenly stand over us. But the young man will say: "I have not grown old yet." Do not be deceived. Death is not bounded by fixed limits of age. It does not fear those in their prime, as though it had power only over the old. Learn this from daily experience as your teacher. You see the funeral bier, how unevenly

and at random it carries out every age: today the old man, tomorrow the youth in his bloom and grace, a little later the boy whose first beard is growing, then again the strong man in his prime, and next the old woman together with the girl. Seeing this, let us make ourselves safe against uncertainty. It takes no effort for a wineskin to be emptied of its air when its mouth is opened a little, and it is no hard thing for a man in an instant [to breathe out] his soul [?]

I see that whenever an earthquake strikes, or a famine, or an enemy raid, everyone rushes in haste to the baptistery, so that they will not leave this world empty of grace. What then? Are the many other unexpected afflictions not just as dangerous as those evils? Strokes, fits of madness, sudden choking, blocked breathing, and the like? Do we not see people fall while running? Or eating, and then ceasing from food for good? Or sleeping, and carried off unawares to sleep's brother, death? Make yourself safe against the instability and uncertainty of life. Do not try to bargain with grace, or you may lose the gift. Run up only such debts as can be forgiven, debts that will not shut you out from the king's kindness. For when the rulers of the earth catch someone who has squandered public funds beyond all bounds and gorged himself on the royal treasury, they give up hope of repayment and punish him bitterly instead, content with penalties in place of the money. You have given many years to pleasure; give some leisure to philosophy as well. Strip off the old man like a filthy garment: that shameful thing, full of disgrace, patched together from a multitude of sins and stitched round with the pitiful rags of lawlessness. Receive instead the garment of incorruption, which Christ spreads out and offers you. Do not push the gift away, or you will insult the giver. You have wallowed in the mire a long time. Hurry, O man, to my Jordan, not at John's call but at Christ's urging. For the river of grace flows everywhere. It does not have its springs in Palestine and then vanish into the neighboring sea. It encircles the whole world and flows into paradise, running in the opposite direction to the four rivers that flow out from there, and it carries into paradise things far more precious than those carried out of it. Those rivers carry spices, crops and the growth of the earth, but this one carries in human beings, offspring of the Spirit. Wherever you draw it, it flows there. It is channeled to the whole world, and its stream is not used up by being divided. For it has a rich spring in Christ, and flowing from him it floods the whole world like a sea. It is sweet and good to drink, and carries along none of the unpleasant brine. It is sweetened by the coming of the Spirit, as the bitter spring was sweetened by the touch of the wood. The pious can wade across it, but for the profane it is deep [?]. Imitate Joshua the son of Nun. Carry

the Gospel as he carried the ark. Leave the wilderness, that is, sin. Cross the Jordan. Hurry to the life according to Christ, to the land rich in fruits that gladden, the land that flows, as promised, with milk and honey. Throw down Jericho, your old habit, and do not leave it a stronghold. Tear down from its foundations the mother of sinful thoughts. Make the deceitful Gibeonites servants of Israel, that is, make your wicked thoughts slaves of the life according to the Gospel. Let Achar be stoned, the crafty and greedy man who stole the tongue of gold. That man is the one [?] who has destroyed the keeping of the precious commandment. All those things are a type of us, all are foreshadowings of what is now coming to light. So send out of your life the gluttonous raven, and give the dove time to fly down upon you. Jesus was the first to bring her down from heaven in figure: the guileless one, the gentlest, the most fruitful. Whenever she finds a man cleansed like a well-kept dovecote [?], she makes her home there, and as she broods she sets the soul aglow and bears many lovely young of her own. These are good deeds and dignified words, faith, piety, righteousness, self-control, chastity and purity. These are the children of the Spirit, and our own possessions. How long will you remain a pupil of the first letters? Open your soul like a writing tablet and let us engrave on it the perfect lesson. Do not lisp forever with the children. Do not be childish in mind. I blush for you: now that you have grown old, you are still sent out with the catechumens like a foolish little boy who cannot keep a secret, when the mystery is about to be spoken. Join the people of the mysteries and learn the words that may not be spoken. Utter with us what the six-winged Seraphim also sing, together with the perfect Christians. Long for the food that strengthens the soul. Taste the drink that gladdens the heart. Fall in love with the mystery that invisibly turns the old into the young. Imitate the Ethiopian eunuch in his burning desire. The Spirit brought Philip to him, and he took him into the chariot to sit beside him. On the way, as a byproduct of the journey, he learned not only to read the wise Isaiah but to understand him. Through the interpretation he tasted the blood of the slain lamb, like a good hound, and he bayed hard at Philip until Philip led him to the full catch of the prophecy he held in his hands. Then he asked for baptism on the spot and received it. He did not wait for a lodging, or look for a city or village or a holy place. He reasoned wisely that every place belongs to the common Master, and that any water is fit for baptism, provided it finds the faith of the one receiving it and the blessing of the priest who sanctifies it. Do not provoke the one who baptizes by delaying. Do not anger him by putting it off day after day and spending in promises

the time that is flowing away. He may strike you with words like John's, and call you an offspring of vipers, or a deaf asp that grows savage at the voice of the charmer. Or he may show you the axe, sharpened and gleaming, laid at the root of the tree and threatening to cut it down. If one must choose between evils, it is better for someone who has been granted the saving bath to fall into sin again than to end his life without any share in grace. For the offense may perhaps be granted pardon or kindness, and the good have great hope of these. But the other case is one in which salvation is utterly ruled out by a fixed sentence. When I hear the truthful voice saying, "Truly, truly I say to you, unless one is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God," I can expect nothing good for the uninitiated. What pardon can it be right to grant such people? They have insulted the royal grace. They would not accept the cancellation of their debts. They did not revere and embrace the freedom that came to them unasked from heaven, and by despising the gift they dishonored the giver. As for a soul that has not been enlightened or adorned with the grace of rebirth, I do not know whether angels receive it after it is parted from the body. How could they receive a soul that is unsealed and bears no mark of its Master? More likely it is carried about in the air, wandering and roaming, with no one to seek it out, since it has no master. It longs for rest and a dwelling but does not find them. It laments uselessly and repents to no purpose, like the rich man whom purple and fine linen clothed, and every kind of luxury and delicate living fed, as fuel for the unquenchable

I want to tell you also the story of a wretched man who missed the great hope and looked for water in a waterless time. Not long ago, the nomad Scythians made a raid that laid waste much of the country along with its inhabitants, and the barbarians were plundering the outskirts of Comana, our neighboring city. A young man of noble family named Archias, whom I knew well myself, was deeply grieved at his own troubles and at the common ills of his homeland. He went out of the city and the fortress to find out exactly how many barbarians were plundering and what sufferings were taking place, and he fell in with the enemy and was shot down with arrows. As he lay fallen and hastening toward death, he cried out with what strength he had (for he was one of the uninitiated): "Mountains and glens, baptize me! Trees and rocks and springs, give me the grace!" And with these piteous cries he died. When the city learned of it, it mourned this more than the disaster of the war. Those whom disease suddenly overwhelms are much like him. The man who was healthy yesterday, and who was mapping out long years of

life for himself, suffers the fate of the foolish man of old. When it is said to him, as all hope is given up, "This night your soul is being released from your body," there is uproar and shouting. Everything is hurriedly sought at once: the vessels, the water, the priest, the instruction that prepares one for grace. The need demands it, but the disease clouds it over, bringing on violent and unremitting gasping for breath. The uproar is no less than the distress of war. Everyone in the house runs into everyone else and bursts into tears. There is jostling and confusion and a wailing, wordless clamor, as though slaves, relatives, friends, children and wife were tangled together in a battle by night. So while it is still a time of peace, let us order our affairs wisely. Receive the gift of Christ in the leisure and calm of life. Then the one who receives this lofty and incomparable benefit is gladly counted on the roll of the adopted, and all who know him make his change for the better an occasion of special joy and gladness. "But I fear," someone says, "how easily our nature slips into sin, and that is why I delay the grace of rebirth." Your timidity has a fine-looking excuse, and you dress yourself up well in the costume of piety. But one brief question will be enough to strip the stage bare with ease. You say you fear sin, and you are a catechumen. What kind of life are you living, then? A blameless and sinless one, or a life in sin? If it is sinless, why are you afraid of baptism, when you already keep the strictness the law requires even before it? But if your life is impure and unguarded, if you are lingering in lawlessness and through long habit acquiring a settled disposition for evil, then it is plain that you are waiting for your last breath, so that your life may end with baptism received at the final hour. This is a new and strange kind of trade, not in gold and clothing, but a cunning bargain that trades a multitude of iniquities for the cleansing of the soul. Pigs go from mud to mud and make their home in the mire. In the same way, those who live with impurities string one iniquity onto another. They defile themselves with fornication, or scheme at odious adultery, or practice drunkenness, the kindling of evil desires, or pursue the sins that are sisters and kin to these. They fear baptism because it would hinder their pleasures and make them give up their foul enjoyments. So when the one who makes excuses for his sins says, "I am afraid," it is plain that he is not wary of sin. What he wants is for his life in sin to be long. Those who harbor this wicked intention deep inside, first of all, are not even granted the grace. Deluding themselves with empty hopes,

they are carried off unexpectedly, when death overtakes them silently and suddenly like a treacherous thief. And even if God, multiplying his own patience and goodness, does count the lover of sin worthy of the mysteries on his last day, the profit of the business is not as great for such people as they think. They suppose that the kingdom will at once be opened to them, that they will receive some place full of wonderful good things, and that they will be granted honors equal to those of the righteous. But this is an empty hope, which bewitches the soul with a false opinion. As it seems to me, human beings will be divided into three groups in the life we await. I speak broadly for now, without subdividing. The first is the rank of the praiseworthy and righteous. The second is the rank of those who are neither honored nor punished. The third is the rank of those who pay the penalty for their offenses. Where, then, shall we place those who received the benefit of the bath as a burial shroud? Clearly among the second, and even that only by pardon, if we are to assign the lots according to God's own love for humanity. For whoever has through sloth betrayed the achievements of virtue is not free from loss and condemnation, if indeed willful wrongdoing is open to accusation and hatred of what is good is clear proof of wickedness. What great gain will you make, then, by falling outside the kingdom and those promises which eye has not seen and ear has not heard? "I am not punished," he says, "and I do not fear the threats. I am content to suffer nothing terrible, even if I am not shown to have achieved anything noble." That is the choice of a wicked slave, deserving of bruises, chains and whips, who is eager only to escape punishment and makes not the slightest claim to the glory of a free man or the honors that come with distinction. These words are hostile to all the saints and contrary to the holy ones of every age. All of them loved the dangers that came with speaking boldly. They gave up their bodies to those who wanted to cut and kill them in all sorts of ways, and they never lost heart before any contest [?], because they looked for honor in the kingdom of heaven as the prize for their blood and their brave deeds. For the sake of that kingdom Abraham, when commanded, sacrificed his son. Moses toiled through the hardships of the desert. Elijah lived a solitary life with no one to care for him. All the prophets went about in sheepskins and goatskins, afflicted and mistreated. For its sake the evangelists bore the wounds suffered for the Gospel, and the martyrs struggled through the tortures of tyrants. And anyone who is truly rational, an image of God with kinship to what is lofty and heavenly, would not even wish to exist or to rise with those who will come back to life unless he were to be praised by God as a good servant and granted some rewards. With this same intent David makes the deer's thirst an image of his own desire for God, and prays to see the face of God, so that he may

delight in a spiritual welcome. And Paul prays to strip off the flesh like a heavy, burdensome garment, to depart and be with Christ. Both of them plainly had in view that blessed and unchanging gladness. If there is no love for that, then truly everything else, as Ecclesiastes says, is vanity of vanities. So, Christian men, sharers in a heavenly calling, flee every such thought, which is worthy of robbers and criminals. Do not count it a blessing merely to escape punishment. Long instead for the gifts and crowns that God has prepared for the athletes of righteousness. Desire baptism sincerely. Take the talent and add your labor to it, for in this way, according to the parable, you will become rulers of ten cities. But whoever is buried along with his baptism has hidden the talent in the ground, and he will surely hear the words that were spoken to the idle and lazy servant. Even the newly enlightened man, if he does well to join keeping the commandments to his faith, has as yet nothing more than blamelessness. He was a prisoner, liable for countless charges, afraid of the tribunal and trembling at the hour of reckoning. Suddenly the king's kindness came, opened the prison and set the wicked free. Let the one who gave the grace be praised in hymns and worshipped, since in the abundance of his goodness he saved those who had no hope of life. But let the other know himself and live in humility. He should not carry himself as though he had achieved something because he was released from his chains. For release from charges bears witness to the mercy of the one who forgave, not to any merit in the one set free. The one who has received the bath of rebirth is like a young soldier newly enrolled on the lists of men-at-arms, who has not yet shown anything soldierly or brave. He has taken up the belt and pinned on the cloak, but he does not at once consider himself a champion. He does not approach the king boldly and talk with him as a familiar friend, nor does he ask for the favors due to those who have toiled and sweated [?]. In the same way, when you have obtained grace, do not suppose that you will live with the righteous and be brought to share their lot, unless you endure many dangers for the sake of piety, make war on the flesh and the devil along with it, and nobly hold out against all the arrows of the evil spirits. Better still, if you agree, let us take as our teacher on this subject the very words of the Lord that will be pronounced at the common judgment. What does he say? "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you." Why? Not because you put on the garment of incorruption, nor because you washed away your sins, but because you practiced love. And at once the list follows of those who were fed, given drink and clothed. The judge who cannot be deceived rightly judges in this way. For grace is the Master's gift, but a way of life is the achievement of the one who has been honored. Of grace

[?] No one demands payment for what he has received; on the contrary, he is in debt. That is why, once we have been enlightened by baptism, we owe our benefactor our goodwill. And our goodwill toward God is kindness toward our fellow servants, our own salvation, and the careful practice of virtue. So lay aside this empty notion, you who hold back baptism to receive it on your deathbed, and know that faith looks for its sister, a good way of life. May we be found worthy of it, by our own good choice and by the help of God, to whom worship is fitting now and [?]
